newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 11. [CORRECTED 20:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 11. [CORRECTED 20:20 GMT]

text.p: The following stories were reported in Tuesday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* 3Com said its fiscal third quarter results would not meet analysts estimates, sending the company's stock down 13-1/2 to 37-1/4 at the close and triggering a technology sell-off.
* Westinghouse said it would pay $1.55 billion in stock to Gaylord Entertainment to acquire The Nashville Network and the rest of Country Music Television.
* Ford found another car seat maker that would let it resume production of its Expedition sport utility vehicle, which it has been unable to make because of a supplier strike.
* VF Corp is expected to announce a $400 million restructuring effort that includes cutting 2,000 to 3,000 jobs over four years.
* AMR's American Airlines began negotiations with its pilots union to avoid a strike, which would begin after midnight Saturday if no settlement is reached.
* A group of banks led by Chase Manhattan recently completed a $300 million bridge loan to Ecuador's government.
* Calpers, the nation's largest pension fund, included Apple and Reebok in its list of 10 underperforming stocks.

* A federal appeals court has decided to reconsider an October 1996 ruling against Microsoft for unfairly denying benefits to workers by classifying them as independent contractors rather than direct employees.
* The Federal Communications Commission could issue licenses by April for next-generation satellites that would cost $23 billion to deploy.
* The dollar fell after the G-7's call to stop the currency's rise.
* The head of NYNEX's telecommunications unit resigned suddenly, walking away from a job he would have had after the company's merger with Bell Atlantic.
* The Securities and Exchange Commission ordered two traders to pay it $2.8 million for allegedly using insider information to profit from Gillette's acquisition of Duracell.
* Days after filing for bankruptcy protection, Jayhawk Acceptance named Carl Westcott as its chairman and chief executive.
* ITT Hartford hopes to raise an estimated $900 million through an initial public offering of up to 20 percent of the shares of its life insurance unit, Hartford Life Inc.
(Corrects to clarify that the company did not provide an estimate of the proceeds from the initial public offering of its life insurance business)

* Electronics giant Motorola has had its troubles, but its hardball tactics haven't changed. By using its muscle recently to get payment of a $35 million bill, Motorola made sure it would come out unscathed from the bankruptcy-court case of its big paging customer, MobileMedia. -- Heard on the Street.
* The difficulties suddenly encountered by used-car lenders Jayhawk Acceptance Corp, Mercury Finance Co and Olympic Financial Ltd are causing asset-backed security
